title: Stravinsky’s Missing Symphony — public composition log
scope: The log the composing agent (Claude) kept while writing this work: the request, its progress messages, the commands it ran on the score and their output, draft publications and test results, up to the publication step. It was written during the work, entry by entry; it is not an automatic export of the whole session, and the same session composed other works whose entries are not included here.
policy: Messages and tool output are recorded as they occurred, shortened where marked. Private internal reasoning, credentials, access details, private paths and unrelated conversation are not included. Statements made during the work may be provisional or mistaken; later corrections remain in the log.

entries.speaker: User
entries.text:
[A long batch brief was pasted: compose and publish one original symphony for each composer in the Missing Works catalogue who has no completed symphony, one composer at a time, claiming each open symphony request through the admin command, publishing live drafts early, testing every movement in the real browser player, writing a notebook and a public composition log, deploying an atomic release, and completing the request only after the public work is verified. Every work must be labelled an original AI-composed homage.]

NOW I know I said to do all composers, but how about we actually do half of the composers in each section? just to save some money.
notes: the pasted batch brief is summarised in brackets; the last sentence is verbatim

entries.speaker: Claude
entries.text:
Composition brief — Stravinsky’s Missing Symphony (work id stravinsky-symphony-1)

Stravinsky wrote several works called symphony, among them the Symphony in C and the Symphony in Three Movements. This is a new short “Symphony in G” in the manner of his neoclassical years. No theme is taken from him.

Orchestra (14 staves, sounding pitch): pairs of flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons, four horns, two trumpets, three trombones, timpani, piano, strings.

Method: the music is built from short blocks, each in one metre and one texture, set side by side without transitions and returning in changed order; ostinatos; a pulse that stays constant while the metre changes (4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 3/8); mostly white-note harmony with added seconds, sixths and sevenths; dry, detached string writing, prominent winds, and the piano as a percussive member of the orchestra. Half-step clashes inside chords and parallel motion are part of the style and are not reported by the checks for this work.

Movements
I. Allegro, G: a motto of three repeated notes; a rocking woodwind figure in 3/4; a trumpet fanfare in 2/4; a clarinet song in D; a middle part with a short fugato on the motto; return and abrupt close.
II. Andante, E minor: flute and clarinet arabesques over plucked strings, around a bowed chorale in 3/4.
III. Allegretto: a six-bar cycle that alternates 2/4 and 3/8, with two short mock-waltzes for bassoon and clarinet.
IV. Largo – Allegro – Largo: a chorale for winds and brass frames a fast movement on an ostinato; the symphony ends quietly on the chorale.

Target length about eight or nine minutes. Compromise known from the start: tunes, the fugato, chorale and the chord of every bar are written by hand; a program writes the ostinato accompaniments, held chords, piano chords and full-orchestra textures from the chord plan.

First playable draft: the whole first movement, built from short blocks in 4/4, 3/4 and 2/4 — a three-note motto, a rocking woodwind figure, a trumpet fanfare, a clarinet song, and a fugato on the motto in the middle.

First complete draft: added the Andante of woodwind arabesques over plucked strings, the Allegretto that alternates 2/4 and 3/8, and the finale framed by a wind chorale. A revision pass follows.

Revision: the Allegretto gains two cycles for the piano alone over plucked basses. This revision matches the published score.
